52|BACKGROUND
53|Apalutamide is an inhibitor of the ligand-binding domain of the androgen receptor.
54|Whether the addition of apalutamide to androgen-deprivation therapy (ADT) would
55|prolong radiographic progression-free survival and overall survival as compared with
56|placebo plus ADT among patients with metastatic, castration-sensitive prostate cancer
57|has not been determined.
58|METHODS
59|In this double-blind, phase 3 trial, we randomly assigned patients with metastatic,
60|castration-sensitive prostate cancer to receive apalutamide (240 mg per day) or placebo,
61|added to ADT. Previous treatment for localized disease and previous docetaxel therapy
62|were allowed. The primary end points were radiographic progression-free survival and
63|overall survival.
64|RESULTS
65|A total of 525 patients were assigned to receive apalutamide plus ADT and 527 to receive
66|placebo plus ADT. The median age was 68 years. A total of 16.4% of the patients had
67|undergone prostatectomy or received radiotherapy for localized disease, and 10.7%
68|had received previous docetaxel therapy; 62.7% had high-volume disease, and 37.3% had
69|low-volume disease. At the first interim analysis, with a median of 22.7 months of follow-
70|up, the percentage of patients with radiographic progression-free survival at 24 months
71|was 68.2% in the apalutamide group and 47.5% in the placebo group (hazard ratio for
72|radiographic progression or death, 0.48; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.39 to 0.60;
73|P<0.001). Overall survival at 24 months was also greater with apalutamide than with
74|placebo (82.4% in the apalutamide group vs. 73.5% in the placebo group; hazard ratio
75|for death, 0.67; 95% CI, 0.51 to 0.89; P = 0.005). The frequency of grade 3 or 4 adverse
76|events was 42.2% in the apalutamide group and 40.8% in the placebo group; rash was
77|more common in the apalutamide group.
78|CONCLUSIONS
79|In this trial involving patients with metastatic, castration-sensitive prostate cancer,
80|overall survival and radiographic progression-free survival were significantly longer
81|with the addition of apalutamide to ADT than with placebo plus ADT, and the side-
82|effect profile did not differ substantially between the two groups. (Funded by Janssen
83|Research and Development; TITAN ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT02489318.)

4|T
5|he initial treatment for metastat-
6|ic prostate cancer is androgen-deprivation
7|therapy (ADT) through medical or surgical
8|castration. In the past few years, results from
9|several large, randomized, phase 3 clinical trials
10|have shown longer survival, particularly among
11|patients with high-risk or high-volume disease,
12|when ADT was combined with either abiraterone
13|acetate plus prednisone or docetaxel for meta-
14|static prostate cancer at the time of initial ADT
15|administration when the disease is castration
16|sensitive.1-7 However, patient age, coexisting con-
17|ditions, extent of disease, and preferences may
18|affect decisions to initiate chemotherapy such as
19|docetaxel.8,9 Treatment with abiraterone acetate
20|requires coadministration of prednisone to pre-
21|vent increases in corticotropin and may cause ad-
22|verse events related to mineralocorticoid excess
23|and liver toxicity.
24|Direct inhibition of the androgen receptor in
25|addition to ADT may provide more a complete
26|blockade of androgen signaling than ADT alone,
27|leading to improved patient outcomes. Apaluta
28|mide, an oral nonsteroidal antiandrogen agent
29|that binds directly to the ligand-binding domain
30|of the androgen receptor and prevents androgen-
31|receptor translocation, DNA binding, and andro-
32|gen receptor-mediated transcription,10 has been
33|approved in the United States and European
34|Union for the treatment of patients with non-
35|metastatic, castration-resistant prostate cancer.
36|The Targeted Investigational Treatment Analysis
37|of Novel Anti-androgen (TITAN) trial was con-
38|ducted to determine whether apalutamide would
39|result in longer radiographic progression-free
40|survival and overall survival than placebo with
41|an acceptable safety profile and health-related
42|quality of life among patients with metastatic,
43|castration-sensitive prostate cancer who were
44|receiving concomitant ADT.
45|Methods
46|Trial Design and Conduct
47|The TITAN trial was a phase 3, randomized,
48|double-blind, placebo-controlled, multinational
49|trial involving patients with metastatic, castration-
50|sensitive prostate cancer. The protocol and the
51|statistical analysis plan are available with the
52|full text of this article at NEJM.org. The trial was
53|designed by the sponsor, Janssen Research and
54|Development, with input from the first author
55|and the protocol steering committee and was
56|conducted at 260 sites in 23 countries. Review
57|boards at all participating institutions approved
58|the trial, which was conducted in accordance
59|with current International Conference on Har-
60|monisation guidelines for Good Clinical Practice
61|and according to Declaration of Helsinki princi-
62|ples. All the patients provided written informed
63|consent. Patients underwent randomization be-
64|tween December 15, 2015, and July 25, 2017. An
65|independent data-monitoring committee was
66|commissioned by the sponsor to monitor safety
67|and efficacy before unblinding and to make rec-
68|ommendations regarding trial conduct. Data were
69|transcribed by personnel at each site from source
70|documents into sponsor-prepared electronic case-
71|report forms.
72|All the authors assume responsibility for the
73|completeness and accuracy of the data and
74|analyses and for the fidelity of the trial to the
75|protocol. The first author developed the first
76|draft of the manuscript with editorial assistance
77|funded by Janssen Research and Development.
78|All the authors had full access to the data, par-
79|ticipated in data interpretation, and reviewed
80|and approved the manuscript before submission.
81|The investigators, patients, trial-site personnel,
82|and sponsor trial team were unaware of the ran-
83|domization codes until trial completion, recom-
84|mendation by the independent data-monitoring
85|committee, or individual-patient medical need.
86|Patients and Interventions
87|Eligible patients were required to have document-
88|ed adenocarcinoma of the prostate and distant
89|metastatic disease documented on the basis of at
90|least one lesion on bone scanning, with or with-
91|out visceral or lymph-node involvement. All the
92|patients had an Eastern Cooperative Oncology
93|Group performance-status score of 0 or 1 (on a
94|scale of 0 to 5, with higher scores reflecting
95|greater disability). Patients were castration sen-
96|sitive (i.e., patients were not receiving ADT at the
97|time of disease progression11,12). Previous treat-
98|ment for prostate cancer was limited to previous
99|docetaxel use (for a maximum of six cycles, with
100|no evidence of progression during treatment or
101|before randomization), ADT for no more than
102|6 months for metastatic, castration-sensitive pros-
103|tate cancer or no more than 3 years for localized
104|prostate cancer, one course of radiation or surgi-
105|cal therapy for symptoms associated with meta-

4|static disease, and other localized treatments (e.g.,
5|radiation therapy or prostatectomy) completed at
6|least 1 year before randomization. Patients who
7|had received a gonadotropin-releasing hormone
8|agonist within 28 days before randomization
9|were required to take a first-generation anti
10|androgen13 (i.e., bicalutamide, flutamide, or nilu-
11|tamide) for 14 or more days before randomiza-
12|tion. Antiandrogen therapy must have been
13|discontinued before randomization. Patients with
14|severe angina, myocardial infarction, congestive
15|heart failure, arterial or venous thromboembolic
16|events, a history of or predisposition to seizure,
17|or recent ventricular arrhythmias were excluded.
18|Patients were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio
19|to receive apalutamide (240 mg) or matched
20|placebo administered orally once daily, in addi-
21|tion to continuous ADT. Patients were stratified
22|according to Gleason score at diagnosis (≤7 vs. >7,
23|on a scale of 2 to 10, with higher scores indicat-
24|ing higher-grade cancer that may be more ag-
25|gressive), geographic region (North America and
26|European Union vs. all other countries), and
27|previous treatment with docetaxel (yes vs. no).
28|End Points
29|The primary end points were radiographic pro-
30|gression-free survival and overall survival. Radio-
31|graphic progression-free survival was defined as
32|the time from randomization to first imaging-
33|based documentation of progressive disease or
34|death, whichever occurred first. A patient was
35|considered to have radiographic progressive dis-
36|ease if he had either progression of soft-tissue
37|lesions measured by means of computed tomog-
38|raphy (CT) or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)
39|or new bone lesions on bone scanning. Overall
40|survival was defined as the time from random-
41|ization to the date of death from any cause.
42|Secondary end points were the time to cyto-
43|toxic chemotherapy, time to pain progression as
44|assessed by the Brief Pain Inventory-Short Form
45|(BPI-SF; worst pain [item 3] was used for this
46|end point; scores range from 0 to 10, with lower
47|scores representing lower levels of pain intensity;
48|a change of 2 was the minimally important dif-
49|ference14), time to chronic opioid use, and time
50|to skeletal-related event. Definitions of second-
51|ary and exploratory end points are provided in
52|the Methods section in the Supplementary Ap-
53|pendix, available at NEJM.org. A prespecified
54|analysis of data from patients with low-volume
55|or high-volume metastatic, castration-sensitive
56|prostate cancer was planned, and evaluation of
57|the efficacy of the intervention in these groups
58|was a secondary objective. The definition of
59|high-volume disease was adapted from the Che-
60|mohormonal Therapy versus Androgen Ablation
61|Randomized Trial for Extensive Disease in Pros-
62|tate Cancer (CHAARTED)7: visceral metastases
63|and at least one bone lesion, or at least four bone
64|lesions with at least one outside the axial skele-
65|ton. Low-volume disease was defined as the
66|presence of bone lesions not meeting the defini-
67|tion of high-volume disease.
68|Exploratory end points included the time to
69|prostate-specific antigen (PSA) progression, sec-
70|ond progression-free survival, and the time to
71|symptomatic local progression. Second progres-
72|sion-free survival was defined as the time from
73|randomization to the first occurrence of investi-
74|gator-determined disease progression (PSA pro-
75|gression, progression on imaging, or clinical
76|progression) while the patient was receiving first
77|subsequent therapy for prostate cancer or death
78|due to any cause, whichever occurred first. Patient-
79|reported outcomes for health-related quality of
80|life were assessed by means of the Functional
81|Assessment of Cancer Therapy-Prostate (FACT-P)
82|questionnaire.15-17 Raw FACT-P scores range from
83|0 to 156, with higher scores indicating more
84|favorable health-related quality of life. A change
85|of 6 to 10 points in the FACT-P total score is the
86|minimally important difference.15
87|Assessments
88|Patients were assessed for efficacy according to
89|modified Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid
90|Tumors, version 1.1, with the use of CT or MRI
91|of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis during screen-
92|ing (≤6 weeks before randomization) and accord-
93|ing to Prostate Cancer Working Group 2 criteria18
94|(see the Methods section in the Supplementary
95|Appendix) with the use of bone scanning during
96|cycles 3 and 5 and every fourth cycle thereafter.
97|Events of progression were assessed by the in-
98|vestigator. Scans from approximately 60% of the
99|patients were randomly selected for independent
100|central review. Adverse events were assessed
101|monthly and graded according to National Can-
102|cer Institute Common Terminology Criteria for
103|Adverse Events, version 4.0.3. FACT-P assessments
104|were collected on day 1 of cycles 2 through 7,
105|then every other cycle, at the end of the interven-

5|after discontinuation. BPI-SF assessments were
6|collected 6 days before cycle 1, then at each cy-
7|cle, the end of the intervention period, and every
8|4 months for up to 1 year after discontinuation.
9|Statistical Analysis
10|The TITAN trial was designed to enroll approxi-
11|mately 1000 patients. Radiographic progression-
12|free survival was tested first. If the difference
13|between the apalutamide group and the placebo
14|group was considered to be statistically signifi-
15|cant, the alpha was recycled to overall survival
16|on the basis of the fallback method.19 An overall
17|type I error of 5% was planned. A total of 368
18|events of radiographic progression were required
19|to provide at least 85% power to detect a hazard
20|ratio of 0.67 with a two-tailed significance level
21|of 0.005. For the final overall survival analysis,
22|410 deaths were required to provide approxi-
23|mately 80% power to detect a hazard ratio of
24|0.75 with a two-tailed significance level of 0.045.
25|Analyses of overall survival incorporated group-
26|sequential design with an alpha-spending func-
27|tion that was calculated as Wang-Tsiatis power
28|boundaries of shape parameter 0.2. Two interim
29|analyses were planned for overall survival. It was
30|estimated that the first interim analysis would
31|include approximately 50% of the total required
32|events for overall survival at the time of the pri-
33|mary analysis for radiographic progression-free
34|survival. The alpha level for interim analysis for
35|overall survival was 0.009, under the assumption
36|of an overall two-tailed significance level of 0.045.
37|Subgroup analyses were prespecified to assess
38|consistency of treatment effect. If the between-
39|group differences in the primary end points
40|were significant, evaluation of secondary end
41|points was to be performed in the following
42|hierarchical order, each with an overall two-
43|sided significance level of 0.05: time to cyto-
44|toxic chemotherapy, time to pain progression,
45|time to chronic opioid use, and time to skeletal-
46|related event. Demographic and clinical charac-
47|teristics at baseline were summarized with the use
48|of descriptive statistics. The primary statistical
49|method of comparison for time-to-event end
50|points was a stratified log-rank test, with strat
51|ification according to prespecified factors. The
52|Kaplan-Meier product-limit method and Cox pro-
53|portional-hazards model were used to estimate
54|time-to-event variables and determine hazard
55|ratios and associated confidence intervals.
56|Results
57|Patients
58|Between December 15, 2015, and July 25, 2017,
59|a total of 525 patients were randomly assigned
60|to the apalutamide group and 527 to the placebo
61|group (Fig. S1 in the Supplementary Appendix).
62|At the cutoff date (November 23, 2018) for the
63|first prespecified interim analysis and after 83
64|deaths in the apalutamide group and 117 in the
65|placebo group, the median follow-up time was
66|22.7 months. The median number of cycles re-
67|ceived was 23 for apalutamide and 19 for placebo
68|(range, 1 to 37 in each group). The median dura-
69|tion of the trial intervention was 20.5 months
70|for apalutamide and 18.3 months for placebo. A
71|total of 66.2% of the patients in the apalutamide
72|group and 46.1% of those in the placebo group
73|were receiving the trial intervention at the clini-
74|cal cutoff date. A total of 45 patients across the
75|two groups withdrew consent for the trial inter-
76|vention (Fig. S1 in the Supplementary Appendix).
77|These patients were followed for survival and
78|secondary end points, so their data were not
79|missing. A total of 39 patients were either lost to
80|follow-up or withdrew from all further data col-
81|lection; this information is not shown in Figure
82|S1 in the Supplementary Appendix.
83|Demographic and clinical characteristics at
84|baseline were well balanced (Table 1, and Table
85|S1 in the Supplementary Appendix). The median
86|age of the patients across both groups was 68
87|years. A total of 16.4% of the patients had under-
88|gone prostatectomy or received radiotherapy for
89|localized disease, and 10.7% had received previ-
90|ous docetaxel therapy; 62.7% had high-volume
91|disease, and 37.3% had low-volume disease. Pa-
92|tients had newly diagnosed metastatic, castration-
93|sensitive prostate cancer or relapsed metastatic
94|disease after an initial diagnosis of localized dis-
95|ease; most had newly diagnosed metastatic
96|disease. Previous therapies for prostate cancer are
97|listed in Table S2 in the Supplementary Appendix.

8|The overall survival percentage at 24 months
9|was 82.4% in the apalutamide group and 73.5%
10|in the placebo group (hazard ratio for death,
11|0.67; 95% CI, 0.51 to 0.89; P = 0.005), and there
12|was a 33% lower risk of death in the apaluta
13|mide group (Fig. 2A). The treatment effect on
14|overall survival consistently favored apalutamide
15|over placebo, with no significant difference in
16|the effect of apalutamide according to disease
17|volume (Fig. 2B).
18|Secondary End Points
19|The time to cytotoxic chemotherapy was signif
20|icantly longer with apalutamide than with pla-
21|cebo (Table 2, and Fig. S2 in the Supplemen-
22|tary Appendix). On the basis of the prespecified
23|hierarchical testing sequence, the time to pain
24|progression was tested next; because the between-
25|group difference did not reach statistical signifi-
26|cance, no formal testing for further secondary
27|end points was conducted.
28|Other Clinically Relevant End Points
29|The median time to PSA progression was more
30|favorable with apalutamide than with placebo
31|(Table 2, and Fig. S3 in the Supplementary Ap-
32|pendix), and PSA reached undetectable levels
33|(<0.2 ng per ml) in 68.4% of the patients in the
34|apalutamide group and 28.7% of those in the pla-
35|cebo group. A total of 87 patients in the apalu-
36|tamide group and 190 in the placebo group re-
37|ceived subsequent treatment for prostate cancer
38|(first subsequent therapies are shown in Table
39|S3 in the Supplementary Appendix). The median
40|second progression-free survival was longer with
41|apalutamide than with placebo (Table 2, and Fig.
42|S4 in the Supplementary Appendix). There were
43|few events of symptomatic local progression and
44|no substantial difference between the two groups
45|in the time to symptomatic local progression
46|(Table 2). Analysis of change from baseline in
47|the FACT-P score with the use of a mixed-effect
48|repeated-measures model showed that health-
49|related quality of life was maintained with apalu-
50|tamide, with no substantial between-group dif-
51|ference (Fig. S5 in the Supplementary Appendix).
52|Safety
53|Table 3 presents a summary of adverse events,
54|and Table 4 shows the most common adverse
55|events of any cause that occurred from the time
56|of the first dose of the trial intervention through
57|30 days after the last dose. Frequencies of grade
58|3 or 4 events (42.2% in the apalutamide group
59|and 40.8% in the placebo group) and of serious
60|adverse events (19.8% in the apalutamide group
61|and 20.3% in the placebo group) did not differ
62|substantially between the two groups. Most dis-
63|continuations of the trial intervention were the
64|result of progressive disease (in 99 patients
65|[18.9%] in the apalutamide group and 227
66|[43.1%] in the placebo group) (Table S3 in the
67|Supplementary Appendix). Adverse events led to
68|discontinuation in 42 patients (8.0%) in the
69|apalutamide group and 28 (5.3%) in the placebo
70|group (Table S4 in the Supplementary Appendix).
71|A total of 10 patients (1.9%) in the apalutamide
72|group and 16 (3.0%) in the placebo group died
73|as the result of an adverse event (Table S5 in the
74|Supplementary Appendix).
75|Rash of any grade was more common among
76|patients who received apalutamide than among
77|those who received placebo (27.1% vs. 8.5%)
78|(Table 4), and the most common adverse event
79|of grade 3 or higher that was considered by the
80|investigator to be related to apalutamide was
81|rash of any type (6.3%). Hypothyroidism was
82|reported by 6.5% of the patients in the apalu-
83|tamide group and 1.1% of those in the placebo
84|group (Table 4); all events were grade 1 or 2.
85|Ischemic heart disease was reported in 4.4% of

4|and a longer time to PSA progression than pla-
5|cebo plus ADT. In our trial, initial therapy with
6|apalutamide in patients with metastatic, castra-
7|tion-sensitive prostate cancer led to improved
8|clinical outcomes.
9|The intent of the trial was to enroll a broad
10|group of patients with metastatic, castration-
11|sensitive prostate cancer, resulting in the limita-
12|tion that certain patient subgroups were relatively
13|small. For example, although all the patients
14|acknowledged the survival benefit of docetaxel
15|during informed consent, only 10.7% had re-
16|ceived previous docetaxel therapy before trial
17|enrollment. This probably reflects perceived pa-
18|tient fitness for docetaxel and differences in
19|patient choice or care approaches. However, the
20|consistency of clinical benefit of apalutamide
21|across all subgroups is reassuring.
22|The incidence of high-grade and serious ad-
23|verse events did not differ substantially between
24|the apalutamide group and the placebo group;
25|discontinuation because of adverse events was
26|low in both groups. Adverse events were gener-
27|ally consistent with the known safety profile of
28|apalutamide. Rash that was related to treatment
29|with apalutamide was common and was typi-
30|cally managed with antihistamines and topical
31|glucocorticoids, dose interruption, and dose re-
32|duction (see the Results section in the Supple-
33|mentary Appendix). Hypothyroidism was mild
34|to moderate; the condition was monitored ac-
35|cording to thyrotropin level and managed with
36|levothyroxine. The incidence of hypertension was
37|lower and of ischemic heart disease was higher
38|in the apalutamide group in the TITAN trial than
39|in the Selective Prostate Androgen Receptor Tar-
40|geting with ARN-509 (SPARTAN) trial, which
41|showed efficacy of apalutamide in patients with
42|nonmetastatic, castration-resistant prostate can-
43|cer.20 The differences in the incidence of falls
44|and fractures between the apalutamide group and
45|the placebo group were smaller in the TITAN
46|trial than in the SPARTAN trial.20 Health-related
47|quality of life in the TITAN trial was also pre-
48|served, with no substantial difference between
49|the two groups, a finding that supports the feasi-
50|bility of treatment with apalutamide plus ADT.
51|In conclusion, in the TITAN trial involving
52|patients with metastatic, castration-sensitive pros-
53|tate cancer, including those with high-volume or
54|low-volume disease, previous docetaxel use, pre-
55|vious treatment for localized disease, and previ-
56|ously or newly diagnosed disease, apalutamide
57|plus ADT resulted in significantly longer overall
58|survival and radiographic progression-free sur-
59|vival than placebo plus ADT. The safety profile
60|did not differ notably between the two groups,
61|and health-related quality of life was preserved
62|during apalutamide treatment.

questions.wording: Was the allocation sequence random?
questions.official_guidance: Answer ‘Yes’ if a random component was used in the sequence generation process. Examples include computer-generated random numbers; reference to a random number table; coin tossing; shuffling cards or envelopes; throwing dice; or drawing lots. Answer ‘No’ if no random element was used in generating the allocation sequence or the sequence is predictable. Answer ‘No information’ if the only information about randomization methods is a statement that the study is randomized.
questions.source_locator: Full guidance p. 17, Box 4, signalling question 1.1
questions.bias_construct: Whether a random component was used to generate the allocation sequence.
questions.decision_rule: Answer yes when a random component was used; answer no when no random element was used or the sequence is predictable. A statement that the study is randomized alone supports no_information.
evidence_needed: The sequence-generation method, such as computer random numbers, a random number table, coin tossing, or minimization with a random element.
questions.no_information_rule: Answer no_information when the only information about randomization methods is that the study is randomized. Do not turn missing reporting into proof that the sequence was non-random.

Statistical Analysis
The TITAN trial was designed to enroll approxi-
mately 1000 patients. Radiographic progression-
free survival was tested first. If the difference
between the apalutamide group and the placebo
group was considered to be statistically signifi-
cant, the alpha was recycled to overall survival
on the basis of the fallback method.19 An overall
type I error of 5% was planned. A total of 368
events of radiographic progression were required
to provide at least 85% power to detect a hazard
ratio of 0.67 with a two-tailed significance level
of 0.005. For the final overall survival analysis,
410 deaths were required to provide approxi-
mately 80% power to detect a hazard ratio of
0.75 with a two-tailed significance level of 0.045.
Analyses of overall survival incorporated group-
sequential design with an alpha-spending func-
tion that was calculated as Wang-Tsiatis power
boundaries of shape parameter 0.2. Two interim
analyses were planned for overall survival. It was
estimated that the first interim analysis would
include approximately 50% of the total required
events for overall survival at the time of the pri-
mary analysis for radiographic progression-free
survival. The alpha level for interim analysis for
overall survival was 0.009, under the assumption
of an overall two-tailed significance level of 0.045.
Subgroup analyses were prespecified to assess
consistency of treatment effect. If the between-
group differences in the primary end points
were significant, evaluation of secondary end
points was to be performed in the following
hierarchical order, each with an overall two-
sided significance level of 0.05: time to cyto-
toxic chemotherapy, time to pain progression,
time to chronic opioid use, and time to skeletal-
related event. Demographic and clinical charac-
teristics at baseline were summarized with the use
of descriptive statistics. The primary statistical
method of comparison for time-to-event end
points was a stratified log-rank test, with strat
ification according to prespecified factors. The
Kaplan-Meier product-limit method and Cox pro-
portional-hazards model were used to estimate
time-to-event variables and determine hazard
ratios and associated confidence intervals.
Results
Patients
Between December 15, 2015, and July 25, 2017,
a total of 525 patients were randomly assigned
to the apalutamide group and 527 to the placebo
group (Fig. S1 in the Supplementary Appendix).
At the cutoff date (November 23, 2018) for the
first prespecified interim analysis and after 83
deaths in the apalutamide group and 117 in the
placebo group, the median follow-up time was
22.7 months. The median number of cycles re-
ceived was 23 for apalutamide and 19 for placebo
(range, 1 to 37 in each group). The median dura-
tion of the trial intervention was 20.5 months
for apalutamide and 18.3 months for placebo. A
total of 66.2% of the patients in the apalutamide
group and 46.1% of those in the placebo group
were receiving the trial intervention at the clini-
cal cutoff date. A total of 45 patients across the
two groups withdrew consent for the trial inter-
vention (Fig. S1 in the Supplementary Appendix).
These patients were followed for survival and
secondary end points, so their data were not
missing. A total of 39 patients were either lost to
follow-up or withdrew from all further data col-
lection; this information is not shown in Figure
S1 in the Supplementary Appendix.
Demographic and clinical characteristics at
baseline were well balanced (Table 1, and Table
S1 in the Supplementary Appendix). The median
age of the patients across both groups was 68
years. A total of 16.4% of the patients had under-
gone prostatectomy or received radiotherapy for
localized disease, and 10.7% had received previ-
ous docetaxel therapy; 62.7% had high-volume
disease, and 37.3% had low-volume disease. Pa-
tients had newly diagnosed metastatic, castration-
sensitive prostate cancer or relapsed metastatic
disease after an initial diagnosis of localized dis-
ease; most had newly diagnosed metastatic
disease. Previous therapies for prostate cancer are
listed in Table S2 in the Supplementary Appendix.

response_framework.firm_evidence_rule: The definitive versions (‘Yes’ and ‘No’) would typically imply that firm evidence is available in relation to the signalling question.
response_framework.probable_judgment_rule: The ‘Probably’ versions would typically imply that a judgement has been made. ‘Yes’ and ‘Probably yes’ have the same implications for risk of bias, as do ‘No’ and ‘Probably no’.
response_framework.no_information_rule: Use ‘No information’ only when both (i) insufficient details are reported to permit a response of ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’, and (ii) in the absence of these details it would be unreasonable to respond ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’ in the circumstances of the trial.
response_framework.independence_rule: Signalling questions should be answered independently: the answer to one question should not affect answers to other questions in the same or other domains other than through determining which subsequent questions are answered.
response_framework.quotation_rule: Brief direct quotations from the text of the study report should be used whenever possible to support the answer.

traps: A no-hit search describes one lexical query, not scientific absence.
A planned method does not prove conduct; a time origin or analysis population does not prove complete follow-up or equal assessment.
An endpoint label or definition does not prove objectivity, blinding, prespecification, or no alternative analyses.
A treatment assignment or visibly different intervention does not by itself prove that participants or personnel knew the assignment.
Different treatment or visit schedules do not by themselves prove that outcome measurement differed between groups.
Stratification does not prove allocation concealment.

static disease, and other localized treatments (e.g.,
radiation therapy or prostatectomy) completed at
least 1 year before randomization. Patients who
had received a gonadotropin-releasing hormone
agonist within 28 days before randomization
were required to take a first-generation anti
androgen13 (i.e., bicalutamide, flutamide, or nilu-
tamide) for 14 or more days before randomiza-
tion. Antiandrogen therapy must have been
discontinued before randomization. Patients with
severe angina, myocardial infarction, congestive
heart failure, arterial or venous thromboembolic
events, a history of or predisposition to seizure,
or recent ventricular arrhythmias were excluded.
Patients were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio
to receive apalutamide (240 mg) or matched
placebo administered orally once daily, in addi-
tion to continuous ADT. Patients were stratified
according to Gleason score at diagnosis (≤7 vs. >7,
on a scale of 2 to 10, with higher scores indicat-
ing higher-grade cancer that may be more ag-
gressive), geographic region (North America and
European Union vs. all other countries), and
previous treatment with docetaxel (yes vs. no).
End Points
The primary end points were radiographic pro-
gression-free survival and overall survival. Radio-
graphic progression-free survival was defined as
the time from randomization to first imaging-
based documentation of progressive disease or
death, whichever occurred first. A patient was
considered to have radiographic progressive dis-
ease if he had either progression of soft-tissue
lesions measured by means of computed tomog-
raphy (CT) or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)
or new bone lesions on bone scanning. Overall
survival was defined as the time from random-
ization to the date of death from any cause.
Secondary end points were the time to cyto-
toxic chemotherapy, time to pain progression as
assessed by the Brief Pain Inventory-Short Form
(BPI-SF; worst pain [item 3] was used for this
end point; scores range from 0 to 10, with lower
scores representing lower levels of pain intensity;
a change of 2 was the minimally important dif-
ference14), time to chronic opioid use, and time
to skeletal-related event. Definitions of second-
ary and exploratory end points are provided in
the Methods section in the Supplementary Ap-
pendix, available at NEJM.org. A prespecified
analysis of data from patients with low-volume
or high-volume metastatic, castration-sensitive
prostate cancer was planned, and evaluation of
the efficacy of the intervention in these groups
was a secondary objective. The definition of
high-volume disease was adapted from the Che-
mohormonal Therapy versus Androgen Ablation
Randomized Trial for Extensive Disease in Pros-
tate Cancer (CHAARTED)7: visceral metastases
and at least one bone lesion, or at least four bone
lesions with at least one outside the axial skele-
ton. Low-volume disease was defined as the
presence of bone lesions not meeting the defini-
tion of high-volume disease.
Exploratory end points included the time to
prostate-specific antigen (PSA) progression, sec-
ond progression-free survival, and the time to
symptomatic local progression. Second progres-
sion-free survival was defined as the time from
randomization to the first occurrence of investi-
gator-determined disease progression (PSA pro-
gression, progression on imaging, or clinical
progression) while the patient was receiving first
subsequent therapy for prostate cancer or death
due to any cause, whichever occurred first. Patient-
reported outcomes for health-related quality of
life were assessed by means of the Functional
Assessment of Cancer Therapy-Prostate (FACT-P)
questionnaire.15-17 Raw FACT-P scores range from
0 to 156, with higher scores indicating more
favorable health-related quality of life. A change
of 6 to 10 points in the FACT-P total score is the
minimally important difference.15
Assessments
Patients were assessed for efficacy according to
modified Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid
Tumors, version 1.1, with the use of CT or MRI
of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis during screen-
ing (≤6 weeks before randomization) and accord-
ing to Prostate Cancer Working Group 2 criteria18
(see the Methods section in the Supplementary
Appendix) with the use of bone scanning during
cycles 3 and 5 and every fourth cycle thereafter.
Events of progression were assessed by the in-
vestigator. Scans from approximately 60% of the
patients were randomly selected for independent
central review. Adverse events were assessed
monthly and graded according to National Can-
cer Institute Common Terminology Criteria for
Adverse Events, version 4.0.3. FACT-P assessments
were collected on day 1 of cycles 2 through 7,
then every other cycle, at the end of the interven-

989|protocolSection.contactsLocationsModule.overallOfficials[0].role: "STUDY_DIRECTOR"
990|protocolSection.descriptionModule.briefSummary: "The purpose of this study is to determine if the addition of apalutamide to ADT provides superior efficacy in improving radiographic progression-free survival (rPFS) or overall survival (OS) for participants with mHSPC."
991|protocolSection.descriptionModule.detailedDescription: "This is a randomized (study medication assigned to participants by chance), double-blind (neither the researchers nor the participants know what treatment the participant is receiving), placebo-controlled, multinational, multicenter study of apalutamide in participants with mHSPC. The study consists of 4 Phases: Screening Phase (up to 28 days before randomization), Treatment Phase (28 day treatment cycles until disease progression or the occurrence of unacceptable treatment related toxicity), an End of Treatment Phase (until 30 days after the last dose of study drug), and then a Survival Follow up Phase. In the event of a positive study result and notification of unblinding at either of the interim analyses or at the final analysis, participants in the treatment Phase will have the opportunity to enroll in an Open-label Extension Phase, which will allow participants to receive active drug (apalutamide) for approximately 3 years. Participants who are receiving apalutamide in the Open-label Extension Phase may continue receiving apalutamide in the Long-term Extension (LTE) Phase if they will continue to derive benefit from treatment (based on investigator assessment). Participants' safety will be monitored throughout the study."

definitions, group or category labels, quantities, units, and denominators do.

For ordinary narrative, table, or figure Evidence, at least one item must contain
`reported.endpoint.name` and a complete quantitative tuple. A multi-span table
instead needs a cited header and quantitative-row span; the endpoint must occur
in its cited title/definition or header, and each tuple value must occur in one
of the cited header, row, unit, or footnote spans. `Total`, `Overall`, or a
similar aggregate label is not an endpoint name. Follow the tuple rules in
[Specify the Result](result.md).
Repair unsupported leaves with exact Source wording and better Evidence; a
support defect does not make the Result unavailable.

## Ground a Domain answer

Attach each basis to the active question it informs:

- `direct_support`: the passage states the answer premise;
- `indirect_support`: the passage establishes it through an explicit link;
- `contradiction`: the passage conflicts with the premise;
- `context`: the passage fixes scope or meaning;
- `inference`: the passage supplies facts from which you draw a stated conclusion;
- `absence`: an untruncated scoped search found no hits;
- `limitation`: an explicit unresolved premise and stopping rationale, with an
  optional current-Trial search receipt when retrieval provenance is useful.

Non-absence Evidence relationships use a selected Evidence handle, except
`limitation`, which uses an unresolved premise and a stopping rationale. A
directly read passage does not require a search receipt. An
`absence` receipt must
report `truncated:false`, `total_matches:0`, and `condition:"no_hits"`. A
positive search may support a limitation after you inspect the
relevant material, but it cannot support absence.

A relationship label never expands what the passage says. Keep plans separate
from conduct, analysis populations from observed outcomes, endpoint definitions
from measurement properties, and absence of reporting from absence of bias.
Reuse Result Evidence only when its exact premise answers the Domain question.
State inferred conclusions in the answer's `justification`, with the source
facts and any unresolved link. The server checks Evidence identity and structure;
you judge whether those facts support the answer.

## Build a Domain answer

Read this section before the first `validate_domain_assessment` call. Submit
one object for each question on the dependency-closed active path. The object
needs `question_id`, the exact permitted `answer`, at least one `bases` item,
`justification`, `unknowns`, and `counterevidence` for an active question.
Use the question card's `options`; the example values are fictional.

```json
{
	"question_id": "sq:randomization:sequence",
	"answer": "yes",
	"bases": [
		{"kind": "direct_support", "evidence": "eh_0123456789abcdef"}
	],
	"justification": "The inspected passage states that a computer generated random allocations.",
	"unknowns": [],
	"counterevidence": []
}
```

Use a limitation basis separately when the source leaves a premise unresolved.

Use these exact shapes for the three basis forms:

```json
{"kind": "context", "evidence": "eh_0123456789abcdef"}
{"kind": "absence", "search_receipt": "sr_0123456789abcdef"}
{"kind": "limitation", "unresolved_premise": "The captured reports leave this premise unresolved.", "stopping_rationale": "Relevant retrieval was reviewed, but the premise remains unresolved.", "search_receipt": "sr_0123456789abcdef"}
{"kind": "limitation", "unresolved_premise": "The captured reports leave this premise unresolved.", "stopping_rationale": "The relevant section was read, but the premise remains unresolved."}
```

`context`, `direct_support`, `indirect_support`, `contradiction`, and
`inference` use a selected `evidence` handle. `absence` uses an untruncated
zero-hit `search_receipt`. `limitation` uses an explicit `unresolved_premise`
and `stopping_rationale`. Its current-Trial `search_receipt` is optional and
may be truncated. When present, copy the actual receipt returned for the
current Trial. A basis kind describes how the premise is used;
it does not add facts to the cited passage.

## Recover an unresolved premise

Use this gap-directed Reason–Act loop when inspected Evidence leaves a material
fact unresolved. Keep the loop in one working assessment across searches and
cursors.

questions.wording: Were participants aware of their assigned intervention during the trial?
questions.official_guidance: If participants are aware of their assigned intervention it is more likely that health-related behaviours will differ between the intervention groups. Blinding participants, most commonly through use of a placebo or sham intervention, may prevent such differences. If participants experienced side effects or toxicities that they knew to be specific to one of the interventions, answer this question ‘Yes’ or ‘Probably yes’.
questions.source_locator: Full guidance p. 28, Box 6, signalling question 2.1
questions.bias_construct: Whether participants were aware of their assigned intervention during the trial.
questions.decision_rule: Answer yes or probably yes when participants knew their assignment, including when intervention-specific side effects or toxicities revealed it. Blinding participants, commonly with placebo or sham intervention, may prevent such differences.
evidence_needed: A direct report of participant blinding, open-label conduct, or participant knowledge during the trial.
questions.no_information_rule: Use no_information only after considering direct facts, indirect evidence, and trial circumstances; an absent explicit awareness statement alone is insufficient when those facts support a probable judgment.

answer_anchors.text: Participants were aware of their assigned intervention.
Participants were blinded to their assigned intervention.

considerations: Awareness is about knowledge of assignment, not whether participants completed or received treatment.

Statistical Analysis
The TITAN trial was designed to enroll approxi-
mately 1000 patients. Radiographic progression-
free survival was tested first. If the difference
between the apalutamide group and the placebo
group was considered to be statistically signifi-
cant, the alpha was recycled to overall survival
on the basis of the fallback method.19 An overall
type I error of 5% was planned. A total of 368
events of radiographic progression were required
to provide at least 85% power to detect a hazard
ratio of 0.67 with a two-tailed significance level
of 0.005. For the final overall survival analysis,
410 deaths were required to provide approxi-
mately 80% power to detect a hazard ratio of
0.75 with a two-tailed significance level of 0.045.
Analyses of overall survival incorporated group-
sequential design with an alpha-spending func-
tion that was calculated as Wang-Tsiatis power
boundaries of shape parameter 0.2. Two interim
analyses were planned for overall survival. It was
estimated that the first interim analysis would
include approximately 50% of the total required
events for overall survival at the time of the pri-
mary analysis for radiographic progression-free
survival. The alpha level for interim analysis for
overall survival was 0.009, under the assumption
of an overall two-tailed significance level of 0.045.
Subgroup analyses were prespecified to assess
consistency of treatment effect. If the between-
group differences in the primary end points
were significant, evaluation of secondary end
points was to be performed in the following
hierarchical order, each with an overall two-
sided significance level of 0.05: time to cyto-
toxic chemotherapy, time to pain progression,
time to chronic opioid use, and time to skeletal-
related event. Demographic and clinical charac-
teristics at baseline were summarized with the use
of descriptive statistics. The primary statistical
method of comparison for time-to-event end
points was a stratified log-rank test, with strat
ification according to prespecified factors. The
Kaplan-Meier product-limit method and Cox pro-
portional-hazards model were used to estimate
time-to-event variables and determine hazard
ratios and associated confidence intervals.
Results
Patients
Between December 15, 2015, and July 25, 2017,
a total of 525 patients were randomly assigned
to the apalutamide group and 527 to the placebo
group (Fig. S1 in the Supplementary Appendix).
At the cutoff date (November 23, 2018) for the
first prespecified interim analysis and after 83
deaths in the apalutamide group and 117 in the
placebo group, the median follow-up time was
22.7 months. The median number of cycles re-
ceived was 23 for apalutamide and 19 for placebo
(range, 1 to 37 in each group). The median dura-
tion of the trial intervention was 20.5 months
for apalutamide and 18.3 months for placebo. A
total of 66.2% of the patients in the apalutamide
group and 46.1% of those in the placebo group
were receiving the trial intervention at the clini-
cal cutoff date. A total of 45 patients across the
two groups withdrew consent for the trial inter-
vention (Fig. S1 in the Supplementary Appendix).
These patients were followed for survival and
secondary end points, so their data were not
missing. A total of 39 patients were either lost to
follow-up or withdrew from all further data col-
lection; this information is not shown in Figure
S1 in the Supplementary Appendix.
Demographic and clinical characteristics at
baseline were well balanced (Table 1, and Table
S1 in the Supplementary Appendix). The median
age of the patients across both groups was 68
years. A total of 16.4% of the patients had under-
gone prostatectomy or received radiotherapy for
localized disease, and 10.7% had received previ-
ous docetaxel therapy; 62.7% had high-volume
disease, and 37.3% had low-volume disease. Pa-
tients had newly diagnosed metastatic, castration-
sensitive prostate cancer or relapsed metastatic
disease after an initial diagnosis of localized dis-
ease; most had newly diagnosed metastatic
disease. Previous therapies for prostate cancer are

guidance: Answer every initially active question plus each dependent question whose activation predicate is met by your earlier answers. Extra inactive branch answers are ignored and never committed. Preserve the approved Result target.

Evaluate activated questions in question order. Submit every activated question with a justification, unknowns, and counterevidence. Review the inspected passages against its exact proposition and check material contradictions. Reuse adequate Evidence. When a premise remains unresolved, state the unresolved premise and why you stopped, and use bounded discovery across relevant Sources, including a protocol or SAP when relevant. Inspect returned passages before using them. A limitation requires that explicit premise and stopping rationale; include a Trial-scoped search receipt when retrieval provenance is useful, but a direct read does not require a search receipt. Absence requires a scoped untruncated no-hit receipt.

Cite complete premises for the active question. One passage may support several facts. When an answer depends on separate passages, cite each with its own boundaries. A relationship kind describes the use of Evidence; it adds no scientific fact.

When inference, conflict, or uncertainty connects Evidence to an answer, include a concise question-specific justification. State what the passages establish, what remains unresolved, and why the selected option follows. Any support relationship is host-asserted: the server checks structure, ownership, and exact Evidence provenance but does not independently judge semantic entailment.

Working premise records are source-grounded resumable notes. Reuse them only when the working checkpoint is current for this exact approved Result and captured Source projection; a stale checkpoint requires the stated recovery action and never carries a prior Domain judgment into this assessment.
A definitive yes or no needs direct_support, indirect_support, or contradiction; a limitation or absence alone supports uncertainty, not a definitive answer.

Evaluate activation against your draft answers. If validation reports missing active question IDs, add those questions with allowed answer values and supported bases, then resubmit the complete active set in one validation call. The server commits only active answers.

Apply every reported repair and retain other drafted answers. Add missing questions to the existing answer set. Resolve further activation from the repaired answers before resubmitting. The server ignores inactive answers.

response_framework.firm_evidence_rule: The definitive versions (‘Yes’ and ‘No’) would typically imply that firm evidence is available in relation to the signalling question.
response_framework.probable_judgment_rule: The ‘Probably’ versions would typically imply that a judgement has been made. ‘Yes’ and ‘Probably yes’ have the same implications for risk of bias, as do ‘No’ and ‘Probably no’.
response_framework.no_information_rule: Use ‘No information’ only when both (i) insufficient details are reported to permit a response of ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’, and (ii) in the absence of these details it would be unreasonable to respond ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’ in the circumstances of the trial.
response_framework.independence_rule: Signalling questions should be answered independently: the answer to one question should not affect answers to other questions in the same or other domains other than through determining which subsequent questions are answered.
response_framework.quotation_rule: Brief direct quotations from the text of the study report should be used whenever possible to support the answer.

traps: A no-hit search describes one lexical query, not scientific absence.
A planned method does not prove conduct; a time origin or analysis population does not prove complete follow-up or equal assessment.
An endpoint label or definition does not prove objectivity, blinding, prespecification, or no alternative analyses.
A treatment assignment or visibly different intervention does not by itself prove that participants or personnel knew the assignment.
Different treatment or visit schedules do not by themselves prove that outcome measurement differed between groups.
Stratification does not prove allocation concealment.
data.completion_rule: Ground each active proposition and its uncertainty in inspected Evidence or bounded discovery for unresolved premises. Supply every question activated by the submitted answer path with an Evidence use, scoped absence receipt, or limitation. Inactive extras are ignored.

sections.excerpt: If carers or people delivering the interventions are aware of the assigned intervention then its implementation, or administration of non-protocol interventions, may differ between the intervention groups. Blinding may prevent such differences. If randomized allocation was not concealed, then it is likely that carers and people delivering the interventions were aware of participants’ assigned intervention during the trial.

sections.source_locator: Full guidance p. 28, Box 6, signalling question 2.3
sections.excerpt: Answer ‘Yes’ or ‘Probably yes’ only if there is evidence, or strong reason to believe, that the trial context led to failure to implement the protocol interventions or to implementation of interventions not allowed by the protocol. Answer ‘No’ or ‘Probably no’ if there were changes from assigned intervention that are inconsistent with the trial protocol, such as non-adherence to intervention, but these are consistent with what could occur outside the trial context. The answer ‘No information’ may be appropriate.

sections.source_locator: Full guidance p. 28, Box 6, signalling question 2.4
sections.excerpt: Changes from assigned intervention that are inconsistent with the trial protocol and arose because of the trial context will impact on the intervention effect estimate if they affect the outcome, but not otherwise.

sections.source_locator: Full guidance p. 29, Box 6, signalling question 2.6
sections.excerpt: Both intention-to-treat (ITT) analyses and modified intention-to-treat (mITT) analyses excluding participants with missing outcome data should be considered appropriate. Both naïve ‘per-protocol’ analyses and ‘as treated’ analyses should be considered inappropriate. Analyses excluding eligible trial participants post-randomization should also be considered inappropriate.

sections.excerpt: This question addresses whether the number of participants who were analysed in the wrong intervention group, or excluded from the analysis, was sufficient that there could have been a substantial impact on the result. It is not possible to specify a precise rule: there may be potential for substantial impact even if fewer than 5% of participants were analysed in the wrong group or excluded, if the outcome is rare or if exclusions are strongly related to prognostic factors.

questions.wording: If Y/PY to 2.3: Were these deviations likely to have affected the outcome?

answer_anchors.text: The identified deviations were balanced between intervention groups.
The identified deviations were not balanced between intervention groups.

questions.bias_construct: Whether context-caused protocol-inconsistent deviations were balanced between intervention groups.
considerations: Balance refers to the deviations identified in 2.3 and their potential effect, not to baseline group sizes.
questions.decision_rule: Answer yes or probably yes when the identified deviations were balanced between groups; answer no or probably no when they were not balanced.
evidence_needed: Group-specific counts or descriptions of the identified deviations and their comparability between intervention groups.
questions.no_information_rule: Use no_information when balance of the identified deviations cannot be determined.
questions.official_guidance: Changes from assigned intervention that are inconsistent with the trial protocol and arose because of the trial context are more likely to impact on intervention effect estimate if they are not balanced between the intervention groups.
questions.source_locator: Full guidance p. 29, Box 6, signalling question 2.5
questions.wording: If Y/PY/NI to 2.4: Were these deviations from intended intervention balanced between groups?

answer_anchors.text: An ITT or appropriate modified ITT analysis estimated assignment effect.
A naive per-protocol, as-treated, or inappropriate post-randomization exclusion analysis was used.

questions.bias_construct: Whether an appropriate analysis estimated the effect of assignment to intervention. Compare randomized assignment with the actual analysis population, grouping, reassignment, and exclusions, including their reasons; an ITT, modified ITT, or as-treated label alone does not establish this.
considerations: The question is about effect of assignment, so grouping must follow randomized assignment.
Assess what the analysis actually did, not the label attached to it: ITT/mITT/as-treated terminology is a description to verify against assignment, grouping, and exclusions.

Never-treated participants are not automatically participants with no adverse event or unavailable outcome. Recover the documented eligibility, outcome availability, and exclusion reason before judging the approved assignment-effect estimand.

A post-randomization exclusion of an eligible participant remains an analysis concern whether it happened before the endpoint was measured or after an outcome value was recorded. Record that timing separately: an outcome not collected may also matter to D3, while an observed value omitted from the assignment analysis is not thereby missing outcome data. Judge 2.7 from the excluded participants, reasons, outcome rarity, and prognostic relevance for this Result.
questions.decision_rule: Consider ITT and modified ITT excluding participants with missing outcome data appropriate. Consider naive per-protocol, as-treated, and post-randomization exclusion of eligible participants inappropriate; post-randomization exclusion of ineligible participants may be appropriate when eligibility could not have been influenced by assignment.
evidence_needed: The actual analysis population and grouping rule: who was assigned, who was analysed in each group, who was excluded or reassigned after randomization, and why.
invalid_shortcuts: an ITT label without its population
a per-protocol label without the analysis population
questions.no_information_rule: Use no_information only after considering direct facts, indirect evidence, and trial circumstances; an incomplete analysis description alone is insufficient when those facts support a probable judgment about appropriateness.
questions.official_guidance: Both intention-to-treat (ITT) analyses and modified intention-to-treat (mITT) analyses excluding participants with missing outcome data should be considered appropriate. Both naïve ‘per-protocol’ analyses and ‘as treated’ analyses should be considered inappropriate. Analyses excluding eligible trial participants post-randomization should also be considered inappropriate.
questions.source_locator: Full guidance p. 29, Box 6, signalling question 2.6
questions.wording: Was an appropriate analysis used to estimate the effect of assignment to intervention?

answer_anchors.text: The wrong-group analysis or exclusions could substantially affect the result.
The wrong-group analysis or exclusions could not substantially affect the result.

questions.bias_construct: Whether failure to analyse participants in their randomized group could substantially affect the result.
considerations: This is conditional on an inappropriate or uncertain analysis in 2.6.
Assess potential impact only after deciding whether 2.6 was appropriate; a small or balanced exclusion can have low impact without making an inappropriate analysis appropriate.

Use facts about this endpoint and the excluded participants. Exclusion before outcome ascertainment may also leave outcome data missing; exclusion after ascertainment may omit observed values from the analysis. Neither timing alone settles the possible effect on the estimate.
questions.decision_rule: Assess whether the number analysed in the wrong group or excluded was sufficient for substantial impact. There is no precise percentage rule: fewer than 5% may still matter for rare outcomes or exclusions strongly related to prognostic factors.
evidence_needed: Counts and reasons for participants analysed in the wrong group or excluded, outcome rarity, and prognostic relevance of exclusions.
invalid_shortcuts: a group label without exclusion counts
questions.no_information_rule: Use no_information when the potential magnitude of impact cannot be assessed.
questions.official_guidance: This question addresses whether the number of participants who were analysed in the wrong intervention group, or excluded from the analysis, was sufficient that there could have been a substantial impact on the result. It is not possible to specify a precise rule: there may be potential for substantial impact even if fewer than 5% of participants were analysed in the wrong group or excluded, if the outcome is rare or if exclusions are strongly related to prognostic factors.

n engl j med 381;1 nejm.org July 4, 2019
15
Apalutamide for Castration-Sensitive Prostate Cancer
static disease, and other localized treatments (e.g.,
radiation therapy or prostatectomy) completed at
least 1 year before randomization. Patients who
had received a gonadotropin-releasing hormone
agonist within 28 days before randomization
were required to take a first-generation anti
androgen13 (i.e., bicalutamide, flutamide, or nilu-
tamide) for 14 or more days before randomiza-
tion. Antiandrogen therapy must have been
discontinued before randomization. Patients with
severe angina, myocardial infarction, congestive
heart failure, arterial or venous thromboembolic
events, a history of or predisposition to seizure,
or recent ventricular arrhythmias were excluded.
Patients were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio
to receive apalutamide (240 mg) or matched
placebo administered orally once daily, in addi-
tion to continuous ADT. Patients were stratified
according to Gleason score at diagnosis (≤7 vs. >7,
on a scale of 2 to 10, with higher scores indicat-
ing higher-grade cancer that may be more ag-
gressive), geographic region (North America and
European Union vs. all other countries), and
previous treatment with docetaxel (yes vs. no).
End Points
The primary end points were radiographic pro-
gression-free survival and overall survival. Radio-
graphic progression-free survival was defined as
the time from randomization to first imaging-
based documentation of progressive disease or
death, whichever occurred first. A patient was
considered to have radiographic progressive dis-
ease if he had either progression of soft-tissue
lesions measured by means of computed tomog-
raphy (CT) or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)
or new bone lesions on bone scanning. Overall
survival was defined as the time from random-
ization to the date of death from any cause.
Secondary end points were the time to cyto-
toxic chemotherapy, time to pain progression as
assessed by the Brief Pain Inventory-Short Form
(BPI-SF; worst pain [item 3] was used for this
end point; scores range from 0 to 10, with lower
scores representing lower levels of pain intensity;
a change of 2 was the minimally important dif-
ference14), time to chronic opioid use, and time
to skeletal-related event. Definitions of second-
ary and exploratory end points are provided in
the Methods section in the Supplementary Ap-
pendix, available at NEJM.org. A prespecified
analysis of data from patients with low-volume
or high-volume metastatic, castration-sensitive
prostate cancer was planned, and evaluation of
the efficacy of the intervention in these groups
was a secondary objective. The definition of
high-volume disease was adapted from the Che-
mohormonal Therapy versus Androgen Ablation
Randomized Trial for Extensive Disease in Pros-
tate Cancer (CHAARTED)7: visceral metastases
and at least one bone lesion, or at least four bone
lesions with at least one outside the axial skele-
ton. Low-volume disease was defined as the
presence of bone lesions not meeting the defini-
tion of high-volume disease.
Exploratory end points included the time to
prostate-specific antigen (PSA) progression, sec-
ond progression-free survival, and the time to
symptomatic local progression. Second progres-
sion-free survival was defined as the time from
randomization to the first occurrence of investi-
gator-determined disease progression (PSA pro-
gression, progression on imaging, or clinical
progression) while the patient was receiving first
subsequent therapy for prostate cancer or death
due to any cause, whichever occurred first. Patient-
reported outcomes for health-related quality of
life were assessed by means of the Functional
Assessment of Cancer Therapy-Prostate (FACT-P)
questionnaire.15-17 Raw FACT-P scores range from
0 to 156, with higher scores indicating more
favorable health-related quality of life. A change
of 6 to 10 points in the FACT-P total score is the
minimally important difference.15
Assessments
Patients were assessed for efficacy according to
modified Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid
Tumors, version 1.1, with the use of CT or MRI
of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis during screen-
ing (≤6 weeks before randomization) and accord-
ing to Prostate Cancer Working Group 2 criteria18
(see the Methods section in the Supplementary
Appendix) with the use of bone scanning during
cycles 3 and 5 and every fourth cycle thereafter.
Events of progression were assessed by the in-
vestigator. Scans from approximately 60% of the
patients were randomly selected for independent
central review. Adverse events were assessed
monthly and graded according to National Can-
cer Institute Common Terminology Criteria for
Adverse Events, version 4.0.3. FACT-P assessments

answers.justification: The article describes the study as double-blind and states that participants remained unaware of the randomization codes until trial completion or an authorized unblinding event. However, rash was more frequent with apalutamide (27.1% vs 8.5%), which could have offered some participants a clue. The report does not say that participants recognized this as treatment-specific or that blinding was compromised, so probably no is the best-supported judgment.
unknowns: Whether participants guessed their allocation or recognized rash as specific to apalutamide.

counterevidence.implication: The marked between-group difference in rash could have weakened participant blinding for some participants, although the report does not establish that they became aware of their assignments.

answers.justification: The article states that investigators and trial-site personnel, along with patients and sponsor trial staff, were unaware of the randomization codes until trial completion or specified unblinding. The intervention was also double-blind and placebo-controlled; no evidence indicates that personnel delivering treatment knew assignment during the trial.

For the radiographic PFS outcome, the registry states that the ITT population included all randomized participants and classified them according to assigned treatment regardless of treatment actually received. The article reports 525 and 527 participants randomized to the two arms. This is appropriate for the approved effect-of-assignment estimand.

Statistical Analysis
The TITAN trial was designed to enroll approxi-
mately 1000 patients. Radiographic progression-
free survival was tested first. If the difference
between the apalutamide group and the placebo
group was considered to be statistically signifi-
cant, the alpha was recycled to overall survival
on the basis of the fallback method.19 An overall
type I error of 5% was planned. A total of 368
events of radiographic progression were required
to provide at least 85% power to detect a hazard
ratio of 0.67 with a two-tailed significance level
of 0.005. For the final overall survival analysis,
410 deaths were required to provide approxi-
mately 80% power to detect a hazard ratio of
0.75 with a two-tailed significance level of 0.045.
Analyses of overall survival incorporated group-
sequential design with an alpha-spending func-
tion that was calculated as Wang-Tsiatis power
boundaries of shape parameter 0.2. Two interim
analyses were planned for overall survival. It was
estimated that the first interim analysis would
include approximately 50% of the total required
events for overall survival at the time of the pri-
mary analysis for radiographic progression-free
survival. The alpha level for interim analysis for
overall survival was 0.009, under the assumption
of an overall two-tailed significance level of 0.045.
Subgroup analyses were prespecified to assess
consistency of treatment effect. If the between-
group differences in the primary end points
were significant, evaluation of secondary end
points was to be performed in the following
hierarchical order, each with an overall two-
sided significance level of 0.05: time to cyto-
toxic chemotherapy, time to pain progression,
time to chronic opioid use, and time to skeletal-
related event. Demographic and clinical charac-
teristics at baseline were summarized with the use
of descriptive statistics. The primary statistical
method of comparison for time-to-event end
points was a stratified log-rank test, with strat
ification according to prespecified factors. The
Kaplan-Meier product-limit method and Cox pro-
portional-hazards model were used to estimate
time-to-event variables and determine hazard
ratios and associated confidence intervals.
Results
Patients
Between December 15, 2015, and July 25, 2017,
a total of 525 patients were randomly assigned
to the apalutamide group and 527 to the placebo
group (Fig. S1 in the Supplementary Appendix).
At the cutoff date (November 23, 2018) for the
first prespecified interim analysis and after 83
deaths in the apalutamide group and 117 in the
placebo group, the median follow-up time was
22.7 months. The median number of cycles re-
ceived was 23 for apalutamide and 19 for placebo
(range, 1 to 37 in each group). The median dura-
tion of the trial intervention was 20.5 months
for apalutamide and 18.3 months for placebo. A
total of 66.2% of the patients in the apalutamide
group and 46.1% of those in the placebo group
were receiving the trial intervention at the clini-
cal cutoff date. A total of 45 patients across the
two groups withdrew consent for the trial inter-
vention (Fig. S1 in the Supplementary Appendix).
These patients were followed for survival and
secondary end points, so their data were not
missing. A total of 39 patients were either lost to
follow-up or withdrew from all further data col-
lection; this information is not shown in Figure
S1 in the Supplementary Appendix.
Demographic and clinical characteristics at
baseline were well balanced (Table 1, and Table
S1 in the Supplementary Appendix). The median
age of the patients across both groups was 68
years. A total of 16.4% of the patients had under-
gone prostatectomy or received radiotherapy for
localized disease, and 10.7% had received previ-
ous docetaxel therapy; 62.7% had high-volume
disease, and 37.3% had low-volume disease. Pa-
tients had newly diagnosed metastatic, castration-
sensitive prostate cancer or relapsed metastatic
disease after an initial diagnosis of localized dis-
ease; most had newly diagnosed metastatic
disease. Previous therapies for prostate cancer are
listed in Table S2 in the Supplementary Appendix.

guidance: Answer every initially active question plus each dependent question whose activation predicate is met by your earlier answers. Extra inactive branch answers are ignored and never committed. Preserve the approved Result target.

Evaluate activated questions in question order. Submit every activated question with a justification, unknowns, and counterevidence. Review the inspected passages against its exact proposition and check material contradictions. Reuse adequate Evidence. When a premise remains unresolved, state the unresolved premise and why you stopped, and use bounded discovery across relevant Sources, including a protocol or SAP when relevant. Inspect returned passages before using them. A limitation requires that explicit premise and stopping rationale; include a Trial-scoped search receipt when retrieval provenance is useful, but a direct read does not require a search receipt. Absence requires a scoped untruncated no-hit receipt.

Cite complete premises for the active question. One passage may support several facts. When an answer depends on separate passages, cite each with its own boundaries. A relationship kind describes the use of Evidence; it adds no scientific fact.

State what the passages establish, what remains unresolved, and why the selected option follows. response_framework.firm_evidence_rule: The definitive versions (‘Yes’ and ‘No’) would typically imply that firm evidence is available in relation to the signalling question.
response_framework.probable_judgment_rule: The ‘Probably’ versions would typically imply that a judgement has been made. ‘Yes’ and ‘Probably yes’ have the same implications for risk of bias, as do ‘No’ and ‘Probably no’.
response_framework.no_information_rule: Use ‘No information’ only when both (i) insufficient details are reported to permit a response of ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’, and (ii) in the absence of these details it would be unreasonable to respond ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’ in the circumstances of the trial.
response_framework.independence_rule: Signalling questions should be answered independently: the answer to one question should not affect answers to other questions in the same or other domains other than through determining which subsequent questions are answered.
response_framework.quotation_rule: Brief direct quotations from the text of the study report should be used whenever possible to support the answer.

traps: A no-hit search describes one lexical query, not scientific absence.
A planned method does not prove conduct; a time origin or analysis population does not prove complete follow-up or equal assessment.
An endpoint label or definition does not prove objectivity, blinding, prespecification, or no alternative analyses.
A treatment assignment or visibly different intervention does not by itself prove that participants or personnel knew the assignment.
Different treatment or visit schedules do not by themselves prove that outcome measurement differed between groups.
Stratification does not prove allocation concealment.
data.completion_rule: Ground each active proposition and its uncertainty in inspected Evidence or bounded discovery for unresolved premises. Supply every question activated by the submitted answer path with an Evidence use, scoped absence receipt, or limitation. Inactive extras are ignored.

Apalutamide for Castration-Sensitive Prostate Cancer
static disease, and other localized treatments (e.g.,
radiation therapy or prostatectomy) completed at
least 1 year before randomization. Patients who
had received a gonadotropin-releasing hormone
agonist within 28 days before randomization
were required to take a first-generation anti
androgen13 (i.e., bicalutamide, flutamide, or nilu-
tamide) for 14 or more days before randomiza-
tion. Antiandrogen therapy must have been
discontinued before randomization. Patients with
severe angina, myocardial infarction, congestive
heart failure, arterial or venous thromboembolic
events, a history of or predisposition to seizure,
or recent ventricular arrhythmias were excluded.
Patients were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio
to receive apalutamide (240 mg) or matched
placebo administered orally once daily, in addi-
tion to continuous ADT. Patients were stratified
according to Gleason score at diagnosis (≤7 vs. >7,
on a scale of 2 to 10, with higher scores indicat-
ing higher-grade cancer that may be more ag-
gressive), geographic region (North America and
European Union vs. all other countries), and
previous treatment with docetaxel (yes vs. no).
End Points
The primary end points were radiographic pro-
gression-free survival and overall survival. Radio-
graphic progression-free survival was defined as
the time from randomization to first imaging-
based documentation of progressive disease or
death, whichever occurred first. A patient was
considered to have radiographic progressive dis-
ease if he had either progression of soft-tissue
lesions measured by means of computed tomog-
raphy (CT) or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)
or new bone lesions on bone scanning. Overall
survival was defined as the time from random-
ization to the date of death from any cause.
Secondary end points were the time to cyto-
toxic chemotherapy, time to pain progression as
assessed by the Brief Pain Inventory-Short Form
(BPI-SF; worst pain [item 3] was used for this
end point; scores range from 0 to 10, with lower
scores representing lower levels of pain intensity;
a change of 2 was the minimally important dif-
ference14), time to chronic opioid use, and time
to skeletal-related event. Definitions of second-
ary and exploratory end points are provided in
the Methods section in the Supplementary Ap-
pendix, available at NEJM.org. A prespecified
analysis of data from patients with low-volume
or high-volume metastatic, castration-sensitive
prostate cancer was planned, and evaluation of
the efficacy of the intervention in these groups
was a secondary objective. The definition of
high-volume disease was adapted from the Che-
mohormonal Therapy versus Androgen Ablation
Randomized Trial for Extensive Disease in Pros-
tate Cancer (CHAARTED)7: visceral metastases
and at least one bone lesion, or at least four bone
lesions with at least one outside the axial skele-
ton. Low-volume disease was defined as the
presence of bone lesions not meeting the defini-
tion of high-volume disease.
Exploratory end points included the time to
prostate-specific antigen (PSA) progression, sec-
ond progression-free survival, and the time to
symptomatic local progression. Second progres-
sion-free survival was defined as the time from
randomization to the first occurrence of investi-
gator-determined disease progression (PSA pro-
gression, progression on imaging, or clinical
progression) while the patient was receiving first
subsequent therapy for prostate cancer or death
due to any cause, whichever occurred first. Patient-
reported outcomes for health-related quality of
life were assessed by means of the Functional
Assessment of Cancer Therapy-Prostate (FACT-P)
questionnaire.15-17 Raw FACT-P scores range from
0 to 156, with higher scores indicating more
favorable health-related quality of life. A change
of 6 to 10 points in the FACT-P total score is the
minimally important difference.15
Assessments
Patients were assessed for efficacy according to
modified Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid
Tumors, version 1.1, with the use of CT or MRI
of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis during screen-
ing (≤6 weeks before randomization) and accord-
ing to Prostate Cancer Working Group 2 criteria18
(see the Methods section in the Supplementary
Appendix) with the use of bone scanning during
cycles 3 and 5 and every fourth cycle thereafter.
Events of progression were assessed by the in-
vestigator. Scans from approximately 60% of the
patients were randomly selected for independent
central review. Adverse events were assessed
monthly and graded according to National Can-
cer Institute Common Terminology Criteria for
Adverse Events, version 4.0.3. FACT-P assessments
